**International Copper Study Group Environmental and Economic Committee Twenty Seventh Regular Meeting 6 October 2009, 10:45 a.m. – 1.00 p.m. Lisbon, Portugal** 

**ICSG/EEC27/8** 

# **UN COMMISSION ON SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT** 

_The UN Commission on Sustainable Development will be holding meetings in 2010 and 2011 which will address, inter alia, mining and sustainable development. Members of ICSG may choose to become involved in this process in a number of ways._ 

‐ The 18th Session of the Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD 18) will take place in New York on 3 ‐ 14 May 2010 and review the state of implementation of goals and targets in five areas (below). The May 2010 session is a review year, which will look at what has been done. This will be followed in May 2011 by CSD-19 (policy year) which will be forward looking.  The Commission encourages UN Member States to provide national reports, on a voluntary basis, that reflect developments in the following five areas: 

1. Chemicals 

2. Mining 

3. 10-year framework of programmes on sustainable consumption and production patterns 

4. Transport 

5. Waste management 

There are several ways for governments, industry and industry associations to provide input into the UNCSD process **:** 

# **i) Direct Submission of Written Inputs** 

The CSD Secretariat welcomes inputs that will contribute to the CSD review process.  In submitting written inputs, note that recommendations for policy action will not be considered in CSD‐18 but only in CSD‐19, that is in May 2011. 

# **ii) Participation in Regional Implementation Meetings (RIM) hosted by UNCSD to prepare for the CSD-18 New York meeting in May 2010.** 

Africa RIM: 26-30 October 2009 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia 

- Organized by: Economic Commission for Africa 

Asia and the Pacific RIM 30 November - 1 December 2009 in Bangkok, Thailand 

- Organized by: Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific 

Europe and North America RIM: 1–2 December 2009 in Geneva, Switzerland 

- Organized by:  UN Economic Commission for Europe 

Latin America and the Caribbean RIM: 17-18 November 2009 in Santiago, Chile 

- Organized by: UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean 

Western Asia RIM: 4-6 October 2009 in Cairo, Egypt 

- Organized by: Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia 

# **iii) Major Group Submissions** 

The nine major groups of civil society, as defined by Agenda 21, are women, children and youth, indigenous peoples, non-governmental organizations, local authorities, workers and trade unions, business and industry, scientific and technological community, and farmers. 

The International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) is preparing to submit information to UNCSD as a part of a Major Group (representing business and industry). The Major Groups’ Discussion Papers, one from each of the nine major groups, summarize their sector’s progress in relation to the thematic areas, identify obstacles and constrain

ts to implementation and set out new challenges to be met by major groups to expedite implementation. These papers are compiled through a consultative process undertaken by the CSD‐18 major groups’ organizing partners. 

# **iv) The Intergovernmental Forum** 

In addition, the Intergovernmental Forum on Mining, Minerals, Metals and Sustainable Development will be holding a meeting in Geneva in October 2009 in preparation for the UNCSD meetings. The outcome of this meeting will be directed toward the CSD-18 meeting. 

# **v) Submission by ICSG (and other Study Groups)** 

Case studies and examples of best practices can be submitted through the CSD Secretariat’s website. The secretariat proposes, subject to agreement of member countries, to submit five brief case studies on work previously undertaken by ICSG and the other Study Groups: 

   - The Role of the Study Groups 

   - The Non-Ferrous Metals Consultative Forum on Sustainable Development (NFMCFSD) 

   - Work by the Study Groups on Recycling Rates 

   - The 2003 St. Petersburg Conference on Recycling 

   - The 2009 Joint Study Groups’ Seminar on Energy and Climate Change 

- These five draft case studies are attached for consideration and comment by member countries. 

The secretariat is also prepared to facilitate the formation of a working group of member country representatives to draft a statement to be submitted directly to the UN Commission on Sustainable Development for the May 2010 meeting in New York. 

# <u>Issues for ICSG Member Countries</u> 

- Member countries may wish to comment on actions planned by their governments 

- Member countries may wish to consider approving the submission of the five draft case studies to the UN Commission (see below) 

- Member countries may wish to form a working group, supported by the secretariat, to prepare a draft of a statement by the Study Groups to be submitted to the UN CSD. The draft would be circulated to all member countries for approval with the aim of submitting the statement in early 2010. 

2 

# **Case Studies for Sustainable Development Number One** 

# Title: **The Role of the Metals Study Groups in Promoting Transparency** 

Internet link: <u>International Nickel Study Group</u> ,  International Lead and Zinc Study Group <u>International Copper Study Group</u> 

Scope:  Global Status: Ongoing Timeframe:  Pre-1997 until present Stakeholders and Partners: International Copper Study Group, International Nickel Study Group, International Lead and Zinc Study Group, Member Governments of the Study Groups, Industry Associations, Private mining companies, International Organizations, others Relevant issues: CSD-18/19 (2010-2011): Mining 

# <u>Objectives/Challenges</u> 

The three Metals Study Groups (International Copper Study Group, International Nickel Study Group, and International Lead and Zinc Study Group) share a commitment to transparency and openness. The Study Groups provide a unique forum where governments and industry ar

e brought together to promote direct dialogue and transparency. A major objective of the three Study Groups has been and continues to be the creation and maintenance of this forum. 

One of the guiding principles of sustainability should be transparency in the market.  This is consistent with both the social responsibility aspect of sustainable mining and with the financially sound aspect, since transparency helps to deliver economic efficiency. 

In order to meet these challenges, the International Lead and Zinc Study Group was established in 1959 through action by the United Nations. It was originally headquartered in the United Nations headquarters in New York, but was later transferred to London, and then to Lisbon.  The success of ILZSG led to the establishment of the International Nickel Study Group in 1990 and the International Copper Study Group in 1992. The United Nations system, and in particular UNCTAD played an important part in the establishment of the Study Groups. 

The three groups are organized in order: 

- To collect, process and publish improved statistics on the metals markets; - To compile and publish other information, such as data on industry facilities and environmental, health and safety issues; 

- To provide a forum for consultations on issues of interest to producing and consuming countries and their industries; 

- To undertake economic analysis of markets and related topics. 

# <u>Lessons Learned</u> 

Several examples of best practices and positive results can be drawn from the history of the Study Groups. 

The International Copper Study Group, International Nickel Study Group, and International Lead and Zinc Study Group have developed an extensive range of publications, regular meetings and websites to communicate and disseminate information. These include: 

- Monthly Bulletins of Statistics for each group providing timely statistics on production, trade, consumption, stocks and historic prices of the four metals. These bulletins are 

3 

widely seen as the best available source of information on the metals, and are used by governments, industry and the financial sector in decision making. 

- Annual Directories providing details on the capacity of mines, smelters and refineries throughout the world 

- Semi-Annual forecasts on the supply and demand of the four metals - Regular reports providing members countries and the public with up to date information on economic, environmental and other issues affecting the mining and metals sectors.  Recent reports have, for example, dealt the industry’s response to the economic crisis. 

- Websites for each of the groups, providing information on the metals themselves as well as archives of presentations on wide range of topics, including sustainable development and environmental issues. 

- Regular meetings, held at six month intervals, at which representatives of governments, industry, industry associations, international organizations and academics can exchange infor

mation and share ideas.  These meetings invariably include presentations on sustainability, recycling and environmental subjects. 

- - Each Study Group has established an Industry Advisory Panel (IAP) which receives direct input from industry representatives. 

- Research projects on specific areas of interest to the members, particularly in areas where there is a lack of information on production, use and trade of the metals. Research has also been done on constraints on future supply and on analysis of regulatory issues affecting metals markets. 

# <u>Policy Options</u> 

An important option available to all member countries of the United Nations is membership and active participation in the Study Groups.  While mining and metals processing are of major importance in a limited number of countries, the population of all countries use copper, zinc, lead and nickel.  The creation of a sustainable economy based on renewable energy will of necessity require the use of all of the non-ferrous metals.  In adopting environmental and tax legislation, governments should keep in mind that non-ferrous metals can be recycled indefinitely and that governmental regulations can be used to encourage sustainable use of metals. 

An additional arena for policy implementation is cooperation between the metals Study Groups and other international organizations.  For example, the Study Groups have worked with the Common Fund for Commodities in a number of important projects that promote sustainable use of resources and improved compliance with best environmental practices. 

# <u>Summary</u> 

The history of the creation, beginning in 1959, and ongoing success of the three Metals Study Groups over the past 60 years should be seen as a success on the part of the UN system to address the issues surrounding sustainable development.  Although the vocabulary used in 1959 did not include ‘sustainable development’ there was recognition that the underlying issues needed to be addressed. 

Over the years the Study Groups have been successful in working to achieve positive outcomes in several areas: 

_1. Open and Transparent Mechanisms to Improve Communication_ : The Study Groups improve international communication, consultation, and co-operation on cross-cutting issues relating to metals and sustainable development. The seek to share and communicate credible scientific research and data on metals in a timely manner to 

4 

facilitate decision making by governments, industry and others, including risk assessment. 

2. _Information on Stewardship Programmes:_ The Groups share information on programmes initiated to promote and demonstrate responsible management of processes and products throughout the life cycle of non-ferrous metals (from exploration, processing, use, through to recycling) along with exit strategies for mines and production sites. 

3. _Promotion of Recycling_ **_:_** The Study Groups work to expand opportunities for recycling of metal-bearing products thro

ugh a number of measures e.g. transferring best practice in technology and collection infrastructures to developing countries. 

4. _Information Development and Dissemination for Decision Making_ **_:_** The Groups encourage the tracking and measuring of performance and reporting on economic, environmental and social factors at all stages of metal processing from exploration, mining and production through to application, use, recycling and end of life. 

5 

# **Case Studies for Sustainable Development Number Two** 

Title: **Non-Ferrous Metals Consultative Forum Sustainable Development (NFMSD)** Internet links: International Nickel Study Group ,  International Lead and Zinc Study Group <u>International Copper Study Group</u> 

Scope: **Global** Status: **Completed** Timeframe:  04/1999 to 08/2003 Stakeholders and Partners: Relevant issues: CSD-18/19 (2010-2011): **Mining** 

**Objectives/Challenges** (Max 3800 characters) 

Recognising the important contribution that non-ferrous metals can make to the overall sustainable development of society, the member countries of the International Copper Study <u>Group, International Lead and Zinc Study Group, and the International Nickel Study Group</u> initiated a multi-stakeholder process in 1999 to address issues related to the mining, production, use and recycling of non-ferrous metals.  The process resulted in the NonFerrous Metals Consultative Forum on Sustainable Development (NFMSD) that convened in 2000, 2001 and 2002. 

Among the key issues and challenges facing the non-ferrous metals industry identified by the Forum were: 

Stewardship Programmes: 

Programmes to promote and demonstrate responsible management of processes and products throughout the life cycle of non-ferrous metals (from exploration, processing, use, through to recycling)  along with exit strategies for mines and production sites. 

Community Consultation and Involvement: 

Facilitation of broad and comprehensive community consultation and involvement in the decision-making process. 

Promotion of Recycling: 

Opportunities for recycling of metal-bearing products should be increased through a measures such as transferring best practice in technology and collection infrastructures to developing countries. 

# Research and Development: 

Programmes to develop, share and communicate credible scientific research and data on metals to facilitate decision making by governments, industry and others. 

Open and Transparent Mechanisms to Improve Communication: 

Develop open and transparent mechanisms to improve international communication, consultation, and co-operation on cross-cutting issues relating to metals and sustainable development, particularly the balance between the social, economic and environmental aspects. 

6 

Information Development and Dissemination for Decision Making: 

Tracking and measuring performance and reporting on economic, environmental and social factors at all stages of metal processing from exploration, min

ing and production through to application, use, recycling and end of life. # Lessons Learned Product stewardship is a complementary concept that it aims to demonstrate how a company’s products contribute to sustainability criteria, both in their production and use. Product stewardship recognises that metals and mineral products are part of extensive and complex life cycles, staring with the extraction of primary materials and ending with final disposal, but with the majority of their existence being spent being used and recycled. By attaching sustainability criteria to products, an integrated life cycle view can be taken, and sustainable development performance can be monitored throughout extended supply chains, as products from one business become the raw materials for another. # Policy Options The Forum produced work in a number of policy areas relating non-ferrous metals to sustainable development including community engagement, risk analysis, life cycle assessment and product stewardship. The Forum developed an overall vision for the sustainable development of non-ferrous metals and an approach to product stewardship. Most significantly, the Forum elaborated a set of principles that form the framework for a possible stewardship scheme. This set of principles is intended to define the component elements of product stewardship. The principles are focussed on product-related issues. They are: |**Governance:**|Products should originate from companies that have a corporate
commitment to sustainable development, who look for similar
commitments up and down their supply chains, and who have high
standards of business ethics.| |---|---| |**Communication:**|Transparency and understanding can be increased through the
availability of accurate information, including the need to inform
employees, the community, customers and other stakeholders of the
safe use of metal_products_and appropriate risk-management
measures.| |**Design:**|Good design can build on the unique properties of metals, developing
and promoting metal products and technologies that are safe and
efficient in their use of energy, natural resources and materials.| |**Recycling:**|The target should be optimal recycling of metal products and materials,
aided by product design, technologies and uses that promote efficient
resource use and recyclability.| 7 # **Knowledge:** Advance the collation of data and the understanding of properties of metal _products_ and their life-cycle effects on health and the environment, and support research to further the safe use of metals. Whilst these principles are designed primarily for implementation at a company level, much is dependent upon the contributions and performance of other stakeholders. In particular, government agencies and users need to support the development of sound, balanced and scientifically based legislation, regulations and standards that protect and benefit employe

es, the community and the environment. 

# <u>Summary</u> 

The Product Stewardship Scheme developed by the Non-Ferrous Metals Consultative Forum on Sustainable Development agreed upon a set of guiding principles for Product Stewardship.  The use of a broadly-accepted common set of principles by all stakeholders facilitates the creation of Product Stewardship schemes. It is intended that such Product Stewardship programs can be extended throughout product life cycles and thus integrated with other approaches (such as mine certification) to develop an industry-wide standard. 

8 

# **Case Studies for Sustainable Development Number Three** 

Title: **Joint Study Groups’ Workshop on Metals Recycling - St. Petersburg, Russia** Internet link: <u>International Nickel Study Group</u> ,  International Lead and Zinc Study Group <u>International Copper Study Group</u> 

Scope: **Global** Status: **Completed** Timeframe **:  09/2003** 

Stakeholders and Partners: **International Lead and Zinc Study Group, International Copper Study Group, International Nickel Study Group, The Government of Russia, The Common Fund for Commodities, Governments of developed and developing countries, mining and metals companies, industry associations, UNCTAD, the European Commission, World Customs Organization** Relevant issues: CSD-18/19 (2010-2011): **Mining** 

# <u>Objectives/Challenges</u> 

The theme of the Workshop was to look at metals recycling from a developing world and economy in transition perspective. As countries with emerging markets increase their role as producers, fabricators and users of metals, they will also become significant generators of recyclable metals. The Workshop brought together governments (policy makers/regulators), industry (metal recyclers, traders, collectors), and other stakeholders to examine the challenges and benefits of metals recycling, share experiences with different jurisdictions from around the world and look at metal-bearing recyclable materials as valuable, globally traded commodities. 

Workshop participants identified issues and outlined possible solutions towards the development of national and international policies or strategies to encourage the sustainable management of recoverable metal-bearing materials and resources. 

The workshop was organized by the three Metal Study Groups. Funding from the Common Fund for Commodities (CFC) helped to subsidize the cost. The workshop helped to disseminate information on metals recycling to participants from governments and industry from both developed and developing countries.  Topics highlighted for discussion included: 

- Regulatory barriers to recycling 

- Market barriers to recycling 

- Market transparency: Need for common definitions, indicators, and statistics 

- Product Stewardship and Extended Producer Responsibility 

- Product design for recycling 

- Rebuilding for re-use 

- Restrictions to import and export of metal scrap 

   - Basel Convention 

   - Securing natio

nal supply 

   - Assurance of adequate treatment (including EHS issues) 

- Formal and informal sector 

   - Environmental, Health & Safety issues 

   - Quality issues 

   - Social issues 

- Dismantling of waste products/Collection issues 

- Technology transfer (BAT versus Most Appropriate Technology) 

- Capacity building in developing countries 

- Competitiveness (viability of industry in both developed and developing countries) 

9 

# <u>Lessons Learned</u> 

A key message from St Petersburg recycling workshop was the importance of both economics and regulation in driving recycling activity.   Economics refers to metal and scrap prices. 

Regulation means both fiscal measures and trade policies adopted by governments. Changes or modifications of either economic conditions or the regulatory framework can have significant impacts on the recycling of metals.  The interplay between economics and regulation should be kept in mind as efforts to promote sustainable use of metals are pursued. 

# <u>Policy Options</u> 

The Workshop produced a set of recommendations that may be used to enhance recycling activity globally. 

In the area of recycling policy the issues of Environmentally Sound Management (ESM), waste definition and classification, trade distorting measures and scrap supply deficits were discussed. 

Delegates agreed on the need for a range of flexible policy options that enhanced recycling without hindering current successes and need  for a change in perception to define recyclables as input materials and not wastes. 

Furthermore, the workshop found that: Governments should: 

- Explore the role of Life Cycle Assessment as a tool for assessing environmental benefits and impacts both to develop integrated product policy and formulate regulations 

- In cooperation with other stakeholders formulate robust LCA protocols and models that consider metal properties appropriately and fully encompass metals recycling. 

- Emphasise the contribution of metals recycling to resource efficiency of use 

- Promote metals recycling as a key element in achieving sustainable development 

- Pursue flexible approaches to formulating recycling policy that balance regulatory measures with market based incentives appropriate to local conditions 

- Encourage the creation of collection and recycling infrastructure through the provision of financial and technical assistance 

- Facilitate the sharing of experience on aspects such as materials flow management and recycling policies 

- Facilitate trade in international recyclable materials through addressing trade distorting policies that affect the flow of recyclables 

- Harmonise international efforts to regulate waste management and define globally applicable criteria for Environmentally Sound Management (ESM) 

Industry should: 

- Develop strategic alliances, including with the environment movement, to formulate and communicate appropriate messages on the benefits of recycling to the public, comm

ercial sector and governments 

- In co-operation with other stakeholders formulate robust LCA protocols and models that consider metal properties appropriately and fully encompass metals recycling 

- • Promote metals recycling as a key element in achieving sustainable development 

- Strengthen dialogue between metals producers and customers on recycling issues 

10 

# <u>Summary</u> 

This successful workshop provided an excellent opportunity for the exchange of information between developed and developing countries, and between governments and industry and with other stakeholders. The Workshop was hosted by the Government of Russia and organised by the three intergovernmental Study Groups – the International Lead and Zinc Study Group, the International Copper Study Group, and the International Nickel Study Group with further sponsorship of the UN Common Fund for Commodities. 

The workshop helped to bridge the communications gaps between the various stakeholders. The workshop brought together over 100 participants including representatives from governments (policy makers/regulators), representatives of industry (metal recyclers, producers, traders, collectors), and other stakeholders to examine the challenges and benefits of metals recycling, share experiences with different jurisdictions from around the world and to look at metal-bearing recyclable materials as valuable, globally traded commodities. 

Particular emphasis was placed on issues concerning developing countries and the workshop was structured to give participants the opportunity to discuss recycling policies and practises, recycling markets and information as well as recycling technology and innovation. 

The Workshop generated positive international press coverage and in St Petersburg the Study Groups were urged by participants to ensure that their findings reached a number of key audiences.  The Study Groups responded by targeting contacts in their member countries and within their official international observer organisations with a view to raising the Workshop's findings at future meetings of these organisations. 

A dialogue on the Workshop findings was established with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the Secretariat of the Basel Convention (SBC), the European Commission, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the United Nations Conference of Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the United Nations Commission on Sustainable Development (UNCSD).  A dialogue with industry was pursued through the non-ferrous industry associations including the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) and Eurometaux.  The Study Groups sought to ensure that the Workshop recommendations receive the widest possible consideration and discussion within these organisations. 

The ILZSG Secretariat made a presentation on the workshop results to a meeting of the countries of the UNEP Basel Convention in Geneva on April 29, 2004 

11 

# **Case Studies

for Sustainable Development Number Four** 

# Title: **Recycling Project Team (RPT)- Recycling Rates for Metals** 

Internet link: <u>International Nickel Study Group</u> ,  International Lead and Zinc Study Group <u>International Copper Study Group</u> 

Scope:  Global Status: Ongoing Timeframe:  09/2003 to present Stakeholders and Partners:  The team comprised the International Metal Study Groups (the International Lead and Zinc Study Group, the International Copper Study Group, and the International Nickel Study Group), Eurometaux, and Eurofer. The latter two representing the European non-ferrous metal and steel industries.  Other organizations  that participated in the work of the RPT were the Lead Development Association International, the International Zinc Association-Europe, the Nickel Institute, the European Nickel Industry Association, the International Wrought Copper Council, the European Copper Institute, the European Aluminium Association, and the Organisation of European Aluminium Refiners and Remelters, as well as the International Council on Mining and Metals. 

Relevant issues: CSD-18/19 (2010-2011): Mining 

# <u>Objectives/Challenges</u> (Max 3800 characters) 

The economic and environmental importance of metals recycling and the need to harmonize methodologies to define and calculate recycling rates justified the creation of a cross-metals Recycling Project Team (RPT) aimed at developing a common set of recycling indicators for metals. The International Metal Study Groups (the International Lead and Zinc Study Group, the International Copper Study Group, and the International Nickel Study Group) worked jointly to establish the Recycling Project Team.  One of the major objectives of the Team was to establish a set of Recycling Rate Definitions.  The following definitions were agreed upon. 

# _Recycling Input Rate  =_ _<u>Metal Recycled (from EOL & New Scrap)</u>_ 

_Metal Produced_ 

_Overall Recycling =_ _<u>Metal Recycled (from EOL & New Scrap)</u> Efficiency Rate Metal Available for Recycling (EOL & New Scrap) EOL Recycling =_ _<u>Metal Recycled (from EOL Scrap)</u> Efficiency Rate Metal Available for Recycling (EOL Scrap)_ 

Two subsidiary rates were also determined by the Recycling Project Team to facilitate analysis of some metal recycling sectors if needed. 

_EOL Collection Rate =_ _<u>Metal Collected (EOL Scrap)</u> Metal Available for Recycling (EOL Scrap)_ 

12 

_EOL Processing Rate =_ _<u>Metal Recycled (from EOL Scrap)</u>_ 

_Metal Collected (EOL Scrap)_ 

Note Scrap definitions:  EOL Scrap – scrap generated at the end of life of a product 

New Scrap – scrap generated in the production of new products (excluding home scrap) 

Home scrap – scrap generated in the same process in which the metal is produced and which is used in that process 

# <u>Lessons Learned</u> 

There are environmental and economic drivers to enhance recycling and to develop recycling indicators. 

   - The metal industry and the recycling

industry need such information to identify weaknesses in the flow of recycled materials and to optimise recovery. - At a time when the volume of legislation linked to environmental matters is increasing rapidly, the development of a common set of easily understandable metal recycling rates is desirable to demonstrate achievements, trends and scope for improvement in the recycling of metals and metal products. - Consistent recycling indicators should also help to ensure that metals recycling is encouraged rather than hampered in any upcoming legislation. - Recycling rates are indicators of recycling performance of products, regions or industry sectors. They can be measured at the various stages of the metal life cycle. Depending on the user and his target audience their application may have different purposes: - Recycling indicators may demonstrate the process efficiency of collection and recovery activities. - Recycling indicators are used to track historical, current and future secondary raw material availability to a sector or region. - Recycling indicators are used to demonstrate status and trends in recycling performance of a region, sector, or company. - Recycling indicators are used to calculate statistical ratios to show the extent to which materials in products are recycled/recyclable and/or to highlight the amount of recycled metal which is contained in products or sectors. # Policy Options It is recommended that metal sectors, legal authorities and other stakeholders wishing to calculate or evaluate metal recycling rates refer to the definitions and methodology developed by the RPT. This will minimize confusion and facilitate dialogue amongst the various stakeholders of the metals industry by providing transparency, consistency and hence, credibility. # Summary The group activities led to the development of three key recycling rates: 13 |Recycling Input Rate =|Metal|Recycled (from EOL & New Scrap)
**Metal Produced**| |---|---|---| |Overall Recycling|=|Metal Recycled (from EOL & New Scrap)| |Efficiency Rate||Metal Available for Recycling (EOL & New Scrap)| |EOL Recycling|=|Metal Recycled (from EOL Scrap)| |Efficiency Rate||Metal Available for Recycling (EOL Scrap)| The Recycling Input Rate (RIR) measures the proportion of metal and metal products that are produced from scrap and other metal-bearing low grade residues. The RIR is mainly a statistical measurement for raw material availability and supply to a metal industry rather than an indicator of metal recycling efficiency of processes or products. The RIR has been in use in the metals industry for a long time and is widely available from statistical sources. Major target audiences for this type of “metallurgical” indicator are the metal industry, metal traders, and resource policy makers. However, given structural and process variables, it may have limited use as a policy tool. The Overall Recycling Efficiency Rate (Overa

ll RER) indicates the efficiency with which end of life (EOL) scrap, new scrap, and other metal-bearing low grade residues are collected and recycled by a network of collectors, processors, and metal recyclers. While focussing on the efficiency of the recycling processes, the key target audiences of this particular indicator are metal industry, scrap processors and scrap generators. 

The EOL Recycling Efficiency Rate (EOL RER) indicates the efficiency with which EOL scrap from obsolete products is recycled. This measure focuses on end-of-life management performance of products and provides important information to target audiences such as metal and recycling industry, product designers, life cycle analysts, and environmental policy makers. 

Two subsidiary rates were also determined by the Recycling Project Team to facilitate analysis of some metal recycling sectors if needed. EOL Collection Rate = <u>Metal Collected (EOL Scrap)</u> Metal Available for Recycling (EOL Scrap) EOL Processing Rate = <u>Metal Recycled (from EOL Scrap)</u> Metal Collected (EOL Scrap) 

These are designed to help in the calculation of the EOL Recycling Efficiency Rate and also help identify areas in which recycling performance can be improved. 

Awareness of recycling needs to be promoted at all levels through public education 

There need to be co-operative efforts to increase technical proficiency and to enhance the exchange of information on recycling between countries 

14 

# **Case Studies for Sustainable Development Number Five** 

# Title: **Joint Seminar on Energy Issues and Climate Change Policies Impacting on the Non-Ferrous Metals Industries** 

Internet link: <u>International Nickel Study Group</u> ,  International Lead and Zinc Study Group <u>International Copper Study Group</u> 

Scope:  Global Status: Completed Timeframe:  04/2009 Stakeholders and Partners: International Copper Study Group, International Nickel Study Group, International Lead and Zinc Study Group, Member Governments of the Study Groups, Industry Associations, Private mining companies and financial institutions Relevant issues: CSD-18/19 (2010-2011): Mining 

# <u>Objectives/Challenges</u> 

The Secretariat of the Study Groups identified several issues that merited discussion at elaboration at a joint seminar involving all three Metals Study Groups.  These issues included: 

- The emerging legislative and regulatory framework surrounding carbon trading markets; 

- The response by industry to the emerging legal framework, including the role of industry associations; 

- Alternative approaches to Emissions Trading Schemes; 

- The carbon footprint of metals production; 

- The beneficial role of metals in countering climate change. 

# <u>Lessons Learned</u> 

The seminar provided Governments, Industry and the Study Groups with a range of outcomes.  These included: 

# For Governments 

- An opportunity to articulate their policy objectives and to details of policies 

- Opportunity to re

ceive feedback from Industry Associations 

- Chance to hear other governments and compare approaches 

For Industry Associations 

   - An opportunity to publicize their role and seek recognition of work done 

   - A chance to publicize their awareness of the problem and demonstrate their willingness to interact with governments to search for solutions to problems 

- To find ways to further facilitate their work 

- For the Study Groups 

   - Identify directions for future work 

   - Keep abreast with developing trends in policy making and regulation 

   - Collaboration with industry 

15 

# <u>Policy Options</u> 

The outcome of the Joint Seminar underlined the need for comparative analysis of policy approaches on climate change. It also became evident that it is useful to have a forum for discussions involving the mining and metals industries, energy and climate change, and the Study Groups are particularly well suited to play this role. The discussions highlighted  that there is a need for compiling additional data on the carbon footprint of metals production and use with a view toward having this information available for use in allocations of trading permits. 

# <u>Summary</u> 

The Joint Seminar on Energy Issues and Climate Change Policies Impacting on the NonFerrous Metals Industries provided an opportunity for discussions among a range of stakeholders including governments, the mining industry, metals processors and financial institutions to delve into the details surrounding the legislative proposals designed to confront carbon emissions and climate change. 

16
